title: Proactive model slimming and request triage for high-memory scenarios
creator: Ava Patel
description:
Problem: During mid-day traffic spikes we observe repeated soft OOM conditions on 80GB GPU nodes when long-context chat sessions combine with large prefix KV caches. Existing approaches (eviction + fallback to smaller models) recover but cause high latency spikes and sometimes failed requests for premium customers.

Goal: Implement a proactive, low-latency mitigation that reduces OOM incidence while preserving SLOs for priority traffic. The feature is a two-part runtime mechanism: (1) model slimming: ephemeral, lightweight quantization/activation-sparsity applied at request admission time to reduce working set; (2) request triage: a short-circuiting router that classifies incoming requests by memory-risk and applies soft-fidelity policies (e.g., partial KV materialization, prefix trimming, ephemeral small-model routing) before admission into the regular batch pipeline.

Why different: rather than purely reactive eviction or broad model fallback, this approach performs minimal, reversible transformations at admission to keep requests on the fast path where possible and only escalate to full model swap when necessary. It targets the request boundary to avoid disrupting unrelated concurrent batches and maintains stronger latency predictability for priority tokens.
acceptance_criteria: Max soft-OOM incidents per node reduced by >= 60% under synthetic heavy-long-context load (see benchmark harness)
P95 latency for priority routes increases by <= 10% compared to baseline under same load
No data leakage: ephemeral slimming must preserve deterministic outputs within configured fidelity window (documented tolerance)
Automated canary rollout with metrics gating: canary passes with green health for 48h before region-wide rollout
design_notes: Admission-time classifier: small stateless model that scores requests by expected KV working set and peak activation using features: prompt length, user history tokens, model variant, explicit pinned context, and recent per-node occupancy histogram.

Model slimming techniques: two lightweight options we can apply at admission (a) ephemeral FP16->FP8-style activation quant path using runtime micro-kernels, (b) sparse-activation hint that disables low-importance attention heads for the first N tokens. Both are reversible and applied per-request, not persisted to model artifacts.

Partial KV materialization: for high-risk requests, only materialize top-K most-recent segments of KV cache (configurable K), and mark remainder as 'cold' to be fetched lazily or reconstructed using summary tokens.

Soft-fidelity ladder: define fidelity tiers (100%, 90%, 75%) where the router progressively applies trimming/slimming before resorting to model fallback. Each tier has documented cost/latency trade-offs.

Fallback integration: if trimmed+slimmed request still causes memory pressure at admission, route to smaller model variant with same response schema. Ensure function-calling and tooling compatibility by wrapping outputs in compatibility shim.

Atomicity: admissions decisions and any partial KV pointers must be reversible; we must not modify KV cache in-place until batch commit succeeds. Use ephemeral reservation tokens and checkpoint metadata for rollback.
tradeoffs: Applying slimming may change token probabilities slightly — risk vs benefit: reduced OOM risk and preserved latency for priority users outweighs small fidelity loss for non-critical queries.
Additional admission-stage compute adds overhead; must ensure classifier is very lightweight and batched to amortize cost, otherwise we add more pressure than we save.
Complexity increase in runtime and telemetry (new states: triaged, slimmed, partial-kv) — requires disciplined schema extensions to Console and tracing.
Partial KV materialization introduces potential cold-cache latency for background toggled segments; mitigate via prefetch heuristics and delayed low-priority fetch.
implementation_steps: 1) Prototype admission classifier and simulator in Python harness against replayed production traces (owner: Liam)
2) Implement slim-path micro-kernels in runtime C++/CUDA with flags for safe rollback (owner: Runtime team)
3) Wire partial-KV materialization metadata into batch admission flow and reservation tokens (owner: KV team)
4) Add triage routing rules to smart-router with A/B toggle for canary (owner: Router team)
5) End-to-end integration tests + synthetic stress harness for long-context scenarios (owner: SRE + QA)
6) Dashboard + tracing update: new metrics and per-request labels (owner: Observability)
7) Canary rollout: single region, 1% traffic to start, expand to 10% after 24h, then 100% by gating (owner: Release Engineer)
testing_plan: Unit tests for classifier thresholding and rollback semantics
Microbenchmarks for slim-path kernel correctness and perf (ensure no >5% extra token latency when enabled)
Replay tests against last 7 days of production traces covering VIP customers and long-chat sessions
Chaos testing: induce forced memory pressure and verify graceful degradation and no cross-tenant contamination
Integration canary with rollback automation and postmortem checklist
rollout_plan: Canary 1: internal-only (staging infra) — smoke for correctness
Canary 3: us-west-2, 10% traffic, 72h; run synthetic stress every 6h
Full region rollout after canary health OK; staggered region expansion with 6h windows
telemetry_and_alerting: New metric: admission_triage_rate (labels: tier, node, model_variant)
Alert: triage_rate > 30% sustained for 5m AND node_OOMs > 0 => immediate circuit to disable slimming
SLO dashboards: p95 latency by route and triage tier, OOM count trendlines, customer-impact slices
